chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Wassash, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'There is no objection to the Kawamikhi of the Magians, and there is no objection to their catching of fish.' The approach in these narrations is to interpret them as meaning: 'There is no objection to the catching of fish by the Magians if a person takes it from them while it is alive before it dies.' Their word is not accepted regarding the removal of the fish from the water while it is alive, because they are not trusted regarding that, which indicates that.

key_terms.الْمَجُوس: The Magians (Zoroastrians), a People of the Book
key_terms.كَوَامِخ: A specific type of net or fishing gear used by the Magians
key_terms.لَا بَأۡسَ: There is no objection / It is permissible
key_terms.يَدُلّ عَلَي ذَلِكَ: Indicates that (referring to the specific condition of the fish being alive)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat fish caught by Zoroastrians (Magians) according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) ruling that eating fish caught by Magians is permissible provided the fish is acquired while still alive, reflecting the principle of *istishab* (presumption of original permissibility). The juristic nuance lies in the Magians' lack of full trustworthiness (*amanah*) in the precise moment of extraction from water; thus, verifying the fish's vitality at the point of acquisition safeguards the ruling against uncertainty. This highlights the Shia method of balancing the general permissibility of non-Muslims' catch with specific conditions of trust and physical verification.
